explain.say: Inuit builders traditionally made igloos from blocks of firm, wind-packed snow, cut with a knife from the ground nearby. Good snow is light but strong enough to stand on.

explain.say: The blocks are laid in a rising spiral, like a spiral staircase, rather than in separate rings. Each new block rests on the one below and the one beside it, so it is supported while the dome grows.

explain.say: The walls lean further inward as they rise, forming a dome close to the ideal arch shape. In that shape the weight of the snow presses the blocks together, so the dome is squeezed and has almost no pulling forces.

faq.q: Why doesn't an igloo fall down?
faq.a: An igloo is a dome shaped so the snow's weight squeezes the blocks together rather than pulling them apart. Packed snow is fairly strong in compression, and the blocks fuse together as they freeze.
asks: How does an igloo stay up?

faq.q: What kind of snow is used for an igloo?
faq.a: Firm, wind-packed snow works best, because it can be cut into blocks that hold their shape. Soft, powdery snow crumbles.

faq.q: Why are igloo blocks laid in a spiral?
faq.a: A spiral means each block is supported by the block below and the one next to it, so the builder can place leaning blocks without them falling inward.
asks: How do you build an igloo wall?

faq.a: It is the last block, cut and trimmed to plug the hole at the top of the dome. Once it is in, the whole dome is locked together.
asks: How is an igloo closed at the top?

faq.q: Why is the igloo entrance low?
faq.a: Cold air is heavier than warm air, so a sunken entrance tunnel lets cold air settle low while warm air stays up in the living space. It also blocks the wind.
asks: Why do igloos have a tunnel?

facts: A well-built igloo forms a dome close to a catenary shape, so the snow is almost entirely in compression.
Snow is a good insulator because it is mostly trapped air, which helps keep an igloo much warmer inside than out.
